slides.title: Can = able to
slides.text:
**can** tells what someone is **able** to do.

A fish **can** swim.
A baby **can't** drive.

slides.title: Must = have to
slides.text:
**must** tells what you **have to** do. It is a rule or a need.

You **must** wear a seat belt.

slides.title: Then the plain verb
slides.text:
After can and must, use the **plain** action word.

✓ She can **swim**.
✗ She can swims.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Read the sentences around the blank.
2. Is it about being **able** to do something, or about a **rule**?
3. Point to the words that tell you.

sentences.t: We must feed our bird every day.

example.explain:
**can fly**: birds are able to fly.

**must feed**: feeding the bird is something we have to do.

together.passage: Our class has a pet turtle. It ___ swim very well. It cannot run fast. We must feed it every morning.
together.hint: Is the sentence about a rule, or about what the turtle is able to do?
together.good: Yes! Swimming well is something the turtle is able to do, so we use can.

sentences: Our class has a pet turtle.
It ___ swim very well.
It cannot run fast.
We must feed it every morning.
evidence.stem: The answer was: can. Tap 2 sentences that tell what the turtle is or is not able to do.
evidence.wrong: This sentence is not about what the turtle is able to do. Look for can or cannot.

checks.passage: Students ___ wear their uniform at school. It is a rule.
checks.why: It is a rule, so we use must.

checks.passage: My little brother ___ count to ten. He is very proud!
checks.why: Counting to ten is something he is able to do, so we use can.

options: Omar can to ride a bike.
checks.why: After can, we use the plain verb: ride.

again.title: Able or rule?
again.text:
**Able to do it?** → can
**Have to do it?** → must

Then add the plain action word.
again.example:
Cats ___ climb trees. → able → **can** climb
We ___ wash our hands before we eat. → have to → **must** wash

slides.title: May = permission
slides.text:
**may** asks for or gives **permission**. It is polite.

**May** I come in?
You **may** leave early today.

slides.title: Should = good idea
slides.text:
**should** gives **advice**. It is a good idea, not a rule.

You look tired. You **should** rest.

slides.title: Must or should?
slides.text:
**must** = there is no choice: You **must** stop at a red light.

**should** = it is a good idea: You **should** eat breakfast.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Ask: Is the speaker **asking permission**, **giving advice**, or stating a **strict rule**?
2. Point to the clue words: please, it will help you, it is the law.
3. Choose the modal that matches.

sentences.t: You should drink water on hot days.

example.explain:
**May I** asks for permission politely.

**should drink** gives advice: it is a good idea on hot days.

together.passage: Faris had a sore throat and a cough. His mother took him to the clinic. The doctor checked him and said, "You ___ drink warm water and rest at home for two days. It will help you get better faster." Faris nodded and thanked the doctor.
together.hint: The doctor wants to help Faris get better. Is she giving advice or saying he is not allowed?
together.good: Yes! The doctor gives advice that will help Faris get better, so we use should.

sentences: Faris had a sore throat and a cough.
His mother took him to the clinic.
The doctor checked him and said, "You ___ drink warm water and rest at home for two days.
It will help you get better faster."
Faris nodded and thanked the doctor.
evidence.stem: The answer was: should. Tap 2 sentences that show why the doctor gave this advice.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not show why the doctor gave advice. Find Faris's problem and how the advice will help.

checks.passage: Student: "___ I go to the library, please?" Teacher: "Yes, you may."
checks.why: The student is asking permission politely, so we use May.

checks.passage: It is the law. Drivers ___ stop at a red light.
checks.why: A law gives no choice, so we use must.

checks.passage: Reem wants to do well on her test. Her friend says, "You ___ study a little every day. That is what helped me."
checks.why: Her friend is giving advice from her own experience, so we use should.

again.title: Three jobs
again.text:
**May I ...?** → asking permission
**You should ...** → advice
**You must ...** → a rule, no choice
again.example:
"You ___ brush your teeth twice a day," said the dentist.

It is advice for good health → **should**.

slides.title: Might and may = maybe
slides.text:
**might** and **may** can show that something is **possible**, but not sure.

Take an umbrella. It **might** rain.
The shop **may** be closed on Friday morning.

slides.title: Mustn't or don't have to?
slides.text:
**must not** (mustn't) = it is **not allowed**: You **mustn't** touch the wires.

**don't have to** = it is **not needed**: Tomorrow is a holiday, so we **don't have to** wake up early.

slides.title: Modal rules
slides.text:
1. Modal + **plain verb**: She can **swim**.
2. No **-s** on the modal: ✗ He cans.
3. No **to** after can, may, must, should, might: ✗ You must to go.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Point to the clue that shows how **sure** or how **strict** the writer is.
2. Maybe, perhaps → might or may. Not allowed → mustn't. Not needed → don't have to.
3. Your proof is the reason given in the text.

sentences.t: The sky is cloudy, so it might rain later.
We don't have to cancel the game yet.

example.explain:
**might rain**: rain is possible, not sure.

**don't have to cancel**: cancelling is not needed yet. It is not a rule against it.

together.passage: The school trip to the science museum is on Thursday. Students must bring a signed form by Tuesday. Lunch will be provided, so you don't have to bring food. However, the museum café might be busy, so you may want to bring a small snack. You mustn't touch the glass cases in the space gallery.
together.stem: Which sentence tells something students do NOT need to do?
options: Students must bring a signed form by Tuesday.
Lunch will be provided, so you don't have to bring food.
You mustn't touch the glass cases in the space gallery.
The museum café might be busy.
together.hint: Mustn't means not allowed. Which modal means not needed?
together.good: Yes! Don't have to means it is not needed. Lunch is provided, so food is not needed.

sentences: The school trip to the science museum is on Thursday.
Students must bring a signed form by Tuesday.
Lunch will be provided, so you don't have to bring food.
However, the museum café might be busy, so you may want to bring a small snack.
You mustn't touch the glass cases in the space gallery.
evidence.stem: The answer used don't have to (not needed). Tap 2 sentences that give strict rules instead.
evidence.wrong: This sentence is not a strict rule. Look for must or mustn't.

checks.passage: Take your jacket. It ___ get cold tonight.
checks.why: We are not sure it will get cold. It is possible, so we use might.

checks.passage: Swimming in this lake is dangerous. You ___ swim here.
checks.why: Swimming here is not allowed because it is dangerous, so we use mustn't.

checks.passage: She should to call her grandmother today.
options: She shoulds call her grandmother today.
She should calls her grandmother today.
She should call her grandmother today.
She should to calling her grandmother today.
checks.why: After should, we use the plain verb with no to: should call.

again.title: Not allowed or not needed?
again.text:
Ask: **Would it be wrong to do it?**

Yes → **mustn't**.
No, it just is not necessary → **don't have to**.
again.example:
It is Friday. Students ___ wear their uniform.

Would wearing it be wrong? No. It is just not needed → **don't have to**.

slides.title: How sure?
slides.text:
might / may / could → **possible**
should → **expected**
must → **almost certain** (a logical guess)

The lights are off and the car is gone. They **must** be out.

slides.title: Modals about the past
slides.text:
modal + **have** + past participle

**should have**: a good idea that did not happen. I **should have** studied.
**must have**: almost sure it happened. He **must have** missed the bus.
**might have**: maybe it happened. She **might have** forgotten.

slides.title: Reading tone
slides.text:
Modals show a speaker's **attitude**.

You **must** apologize. → firm
You **might** want to apologize. → gentle

Writers choose modals to sound polite, firm or unsure.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Point to the **evidence** the speaker has.
2. Strong evidence → **must**. Some evidence → **might** or **may**.
3. A good idea that did not happen → **should have**.

The proof is the clue in the text that makes the speaker sure or unsure.

sentences.t: The ground is wet, and there are puddles everywhere.
It must have rained during the night.

example.explain:
The speaker did not see the rain, but the wet ground and puddles are strong evidence.

So the speaker is almost sure: **must have rained**.

together.passage: When Salma reached the classroom, the door was locked and the lights were off. A note on the door said, "Back in ten minutes." Her friend Dana arrived a moment later. "Ms. Huda's car is still in the parking lot," Dana said. "She ___ be somewhere in the school." Salma looked at her phone and sighed. "We should have read the school messages last night."
together.stem: Which word best fits Dana's guess?
together.hint: Look at the clues Dana and Salma have. Are they strong enough for Dana to be almost sure?
together.good: Yes! The car is still there and the note says she will be back soon, so Dana is almost certain: she must be in the school.

sentences: When Salma reached the classroom, the door was locked and the lights were off.
A note on the door said, "Back in ten minutes."
Her friend Dana arrived a moment later.
"Ms. Huda's car is still in the parking lot," Dana said.
"She ___ be somewhere in the school."
Salma looked at her phone and sighed.
"We should have read the school messages last night."
evidence.stem: The answer was: must (almost certain). Tap 2 sentences that give the evidence.
evidence.wrong: This sentence is not evidence about where Ms. Huda is. Find the clues on the door and in the parking lot.

checks.passage: I can't find my keys. I remember putting them on my office desk this morning, and I didn't touch them after that. I ___ have left them at the office.
checks.why: The speaker has strong evidence, so they are almost sure: must have left.

checks.passage: You didn't drink any water during the long hike, and now you feel dizzy.
options: You should have drunk some water.
checks.why: Drinking water was a good idea that did not happen, so we use should have + the past participle drunk.

checks.passage: Teacher A: "You must hand in the report by Sunday." Teacher B: "You might want to hand in the report by Sunday."
options: Teacher B is talking about the past.
Teacher B is gentler, so it sounds like advice.
checks.why: Might want to softens the message. It sounds like a suggestion, while must sounds like a firm rule.

again.title: Weigh the evidence
again.text:
Strong clues → **must** (have)
Some clues → **might** / **may** (have)
A missed good idea → **should have**
again.example:
Ahmad's bag is gone and his jacket is gone.

Strong clues → He **must have** gone home.

He forgot his book → He **should have** checked his desk.
